1 Edge Detection Overview

Core Definition

An edge is a location in an image where the pixel intensity changes rapidly — i.e., a discontinuity in the image's brightness function. Rather than storing every pixel, edges give us a compact, information-rich representation of an image's structure.

Why Do We Care About Edges?

  • Object Recognition: Edges outline shapes, making it easier to identify objects without full pixel data.
  • Geometry Recovery: 3D shape, depth, and viewpoint can be estimated from edge maps.
  • Compact Representation: Edge images are far smaller than raw pixel images — you keep only the "important" locations.
  • Feature Extraction: Most high-level CV algorithms (SIFT, HOG, etc.) work on gradient/edge information under the hood.

Causes of Edges (Discontinuities)

Edges arise from several physical phenomena:

  • Surface orientation discontinuities: Flat faces of a 3D object meeting at an angle produce intensity jumps.
  • Depth discontinuities: Object boundaries against a background — the foreground and background often have very different colours.
  • Illumination discontinuities: Shadows create sharp brightness differences even on smooth surfaces.
  • Reflectance / colour discontinuities: Two materials with different surface properties lit identically still produce edge-like boundaries.

2 Characterizing Edges — The Derivative

Mathematically, an edge is a place where the derivative of image intensity is large. If f(x) is the intensity along a scanline:

Edge ↔ large |f′(x)| = |df/dx|
A peak in the derivative magnitude signals a rapid change in intensity — i.e., an edge.

Finite Difference Approximation

Computers work with discrete pixel grids, so the derivative is approximated with finite differences:

f′(x) ≈ [f(x+1) − f(x−1)] / 2

Or the simpler forward difference:   f′(x) ≈ f(x+1) − f(x)
These correspond to convolution with kernels [-1, 0, 1] or [-1, 1] respectively.
💡

Intuition: Think of the image as a height map. Edges are the steep cliffs. The derivative measures the slope — the steeper the slope, the stronger the edge.

The 2D Gradient

In 2D images, edges can run in any direction, so we compute partial derivatives in both x and y:

∇f = [∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y]ᵀ

Gradient Magnitude: |∇f| = √( (∂f/∂x)² + (∂f/∂y)² )

Gradient Direction: θ = arctan( ∂f/∂y ÷ ∂f/∂x )
The gradient always points perpendicular to the edge direction. Its magnitude tells us edge strength.

3 Effect of Noise on Edges

Problem: Real images are always noisy. Noise causes tiny random intensity fluctuations between neighbouring pixels. Taking the derivative amplifies these — a small noise spike becomes a huge false positive edge.

The Solution: Smooth First, Then Differentiate

The standard fix is to blur the image with a Gaussian filter g(x,y) before taking derivatives. This averages out high-frequency noise.

The Associativity Trick (Key Insight!)

Naively this costs two convolution operations: first smooth, then differentiate. But convolution is associative, so:

d/dx (f ∗ g) = f ∗ (d/dx g)
We can pre-compute the derivative of the Gaussian (a fixed kernel) and convolve it with the image in ONE pass — saving significant computation.

Gaussian Smoothing & Scale (σ)

The Gaussian g(x,y) = (1/2πσ²) · exp(−(x²+y²)/2σ²) has one free parameter, σ (sigma):

  • Small σ: Fine smoothing — detects subtle, detailed edges. More noise sensitivity.
  • Large σ: Heavy smoothing — suppresses noise strongly but blurs fine details and locates edges less precisely.

There is an inherent scale-space trade-off: you choose σ based on how coarse vs. fine you want your edges.

4 Edge Detectors

The main gradient-based edge detectors we study are:

  • 🔷 Prewitt Operator — simple gradient approximation with equal weights
  • 🔷 Sobel Operator — weighted gradient emphasising the central pixel
  • 🔷 Marr-Hildreth (LoG) — Laplacian of Gaussian with zero-crossing detection
  • 🔷 Canny — optimal multi-stage detector (covered in Section 5)

4.1 Prewitt Edge Detector

The Prewitt operator approximates the first derivative using two 3×3 kernels — one for horizontal edges (Ky) and one for vertical edges (Kx):

Gradient Magnitude: |∇I| = √(Gx² + Gy²)

Approximation: |∇I| ≈ |Gx| + |Gy| (cheaper to compute)
Gx = Kx ∗ I and Gy = Ky ∗ I (where ∗ denotes convolution)

4.2 Sobel Edge Detector

Sobel is the most widely used gradient operator. It is similar to Prewitt but gives extra weight to the pixel directly in line with the edge direction (the central row/column gets weight 2). This makes it less sensitive to noise:

Why central weighting? The Sobel kernel can be factored as a smoothing step (1D Gaussian approximation [1,2,1]) in one direction combined with differentiation [-1,0,+1] in the other. This built-in smoothing is why Sobel is more robust to noise than Prewitt.

4.3 Marr-Hildreth Edge Detector (Laplacian of Gaussian)

Instead of using gradient magnitude (first derivative), Marr-Hildreth uses the Laplacian (second derivative). Edges correspond to zero-crossings of the second derivative — locations where the second derivative changes sign.

Laplacian: ∇²f = ∂²f/∂x² + ∂²f/∂y²

Gaussian: g(x,y) = (1/2πσ²) · exp(−(x²+y²)/2σ²)

Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG): ∇²g(x,y) = −(1/πσ⁴) · [1 − (x²+y²)/2σ²] · exp(−(x²+y²)/2σ²)
The LoG kernel is also called the "Mexican Hat" wavelet due to its shape — positive central lobe, negative surrounding ring.
Marr-Hildreth Algorithm
1
Gaussian Smoothing
Convolve the image I with Gaussian g to get smoothed image S = I ∗ g
2
Apply Laplacian
Compute ∇²S. Equivalently, convolve I with the precomputed LoG filter ∇²g directly.
3
Find Zero-Crossings
Scan each row and column. Mark a pixel as an edge wherever the LoG response changes sign.
4
Threshold the Slope
The "slope" at a zero-crossing {a, −b} is |a+b|. Only keep zero-crossings with large slope (strong edges).

Understanding Zero-Crossings

There are four cases of how a zero-crossing can appear in a discrete signal:

  • {+, −} — directly adjacent positive and negative values
  • {+, 0, −} — explicit zero between positive and negative
  • {−, +} — sign flip in opposite direction
  • {−, 0, +} — explicit zero between negative and positive

The slope of the zero-crossing = |a + b| where a and b are the two values on either side. A threshold on this slope filters out weak, noisy zero-crossings.

Efficient Implementation with Separable 1D Filters

∇²g(x,y) = gxx(x)·g(y) + g(x)·gyy(y)
The 2D LoG filter can be decomposed into 4 separable 1D convolutions: g(x), gxx(x), g(y), gyy(y) — much faster than a full 2D convolution!

5 Canny Edge Detector

The Canny detector, published by John Canny in 1986, is considered the optimal edge detector under well-defined mathematical criteria:

  • 🎯 Good Detection: Minimise both false positives AND false negatives. Find all real edges.
  • 📍 Good Localisation: Detected edges must be as close as possible to the true edge locations.
  • 1️⃣ Single Response: Return exactly one point for each true edge point — no doubled edges.
Canny Algorithm — 5 Steps
1
Gaussian Smoothing
S = I ∗ g(x,y,σ) — blur image to suppress noise
2
Gradient Computation
Compute ∂S/∂x and ∂S/∂y using derivative of Gaussian filters
3
Gradient Magnitude & Direction
M = √(Gx²+Gy²), θ = arctan(Gy/Gx)
4
Non-Maximum Suppression
Thin edges to 1-pixel width by keeping only local maxima along gradient direction
5
Hysteresis Thresholding
Use two thresholds (low, high) to retain strong edges and connect weak ones

Step 1–2: Smoothing and Derivatives

Smoothing: S = I ∗ g(x,y)

Gradient: ∇S = ∇(g ∗ I) = (∇g) ∗ I

In components: ∇S = [ gx ∗ I, gy ∗ I ]ᵀ where gx = ∂g/∂x and gy = ∂g/∂y
Key insight: we convolve the image with the DERIVATIVE of the Gaussian, not the Gaussian itself. One convolution achieves both smoothing and differentiation simultaneously.

Step 3: Gradient Magnitude and Direction

Magnitude: M(x,y) = √[ (∂S/∂x)² + (∂S/∂y)² ]

Direction: θ(x,y) = arctan( ∂S/∂y ÷ ∂S/∂x )
θ is perpendicular to the edge. The gradient always points in the direction of maximum intensity increase.

Step 4: Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)

What is NMS and why do we need it?

The gradient magnitude image has thick blurry edges (several pixels wide). NMS thins them to exactly 1 pixel. The idea: at each pixel, check if it is a local maximum along the gradient direction. If a neighbour in the gradient direction has a higher magnitude, suppress (zero out) the current pixel.

For pixel p with gradient direction θ:

Let q = neighbour of p in direction θ Let r = neighbour of p in direction θ+180°

If M(p) ≥ M(q) AND M(p) ≥ M(r): keep p as edge candidate Else: suppress p (set to 0)
In practice, θ is quantised to 4 directions: 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°. Sub-pixel interpolation can be used for better accuracy.

Step 5: Hysteresis Thresholding

The Problem with a Single Threshold

A single threshold creates two problems: set it too high → miss real edges; set it too low → include noise. Hysteresis solves this with two thresholds: T_high and T_low.

if M(x,y) > T_high → STRONG edge (definitely an edge) if M(x,y) < T_low → WEAK / non-edge (discard) if T_low ≤ M(x,y) ≤ T_high → CANDIDATE (keep if connected to a STRONG edge)
Typical ratio: T_high : T_low ≈ 2:1 or 3:1. OpenCV's Canny defaults are often 100 and 200.
Hysteresis Algorithm
1
Scan image left-to-right, top-to-bottom
2
If gradient at pixel > T_high → mark as edge pixel
3
Recursively inspect all 8 neighbours of this edge pixel
4
If neighbour gradient > T_low → also mark as edge pixel
5
Continue until no more connected candidates found

6 Comparison of Edge Detectors

Detector Method Noise Robustness Localisation Thin Edges? Complexity
Prewitt First derivative (equal weights) Low Fair No Simple
Sobel First derivative (centre-weighted) Moderate Good No Simple
Marr-Hildreth Second derivative / zero-crossing Good (σ-tunable) Good Yes (zero-crossing) Moderate
Canny Gradient + NMS + Hysteresis Excellent (σ-tunable) Excellent Yes (NMS) Higher

import numpy as np
import cv2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.ndimage import convolve, gaussian_filter, gaussian_laplace
from scipy.signal import convolve2d

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. UTILITY: Load image and display multiple results
# -----------------------------------------------------------
def load_gray(path):
    """Load an image as grayscale float [0,1]."""
    img = cv2.imread(path, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    if img is None:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Cannot open: {path}")
    return img.astype(np.float32) / 255.0

def show(images, titles, cmap='gray', figsize=(18,5)):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(images), figsize=figsize)
    for ax, img, title in zip(axes, images, titles):
        ax.imshow(img, cmap=cmap)
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
        ax.axis('off')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Section A — Understanding the Gradient

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# A. THE GRADIENT — First principles
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def compute_gradient_basic(img):
    """
    Compute image gradient using simple finite differences.
    Returns Gx, Gy (partial derivatives), magnitude, and direction.
    """
    # Simple [-1, 0, 1] kernels (finite differences)
    kernel_x = np.array([[-1, 0, 1],
                          [-1, 0, 1],
                          [-1, 0, 1]], dtype=np.float32)
    kernel_y = np.array([[-1, -1, -1],
                          [ 0,  0,  0],
                          [ 1,  1,  1]], dtype=np.float32)

    Gx = convolve(img, kernel_x)   # horizontal gradient
    Gy = convolve(img, kernel_y)   # vertical gradient

    magnitude  = np.sqrt(Gx**2 + Gy**2)  # |∇f|
    direction  = np.arctan2(Gy, Gx)        # θ = arctan(Gy/Gx)

    return Gx, Gy, magnitude, direction

# Usage:
# img = load_gray('your_image.jpg')
# Gx, Gy, mag, theta = compute_gradient_basic(img)
# show([img, mag], ['Original', 'Gradient Magnitude'])

Section B — Prewitt Detector

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# B. PREWITT EDGE DETECTOR
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def prewitt_detector(img, threshold=0.1):
    """
    Prewitt edge detector.
    Parameters:
        img       : grayscale float image [0,1]
        threshold : gradient magnitude threshold for edge binarisation
    Returns:
        Gx, Gy   : gradient components
        magnitude: gradient magnitude
        edges    : binary edge map
    """
    # Prewitt kernels — equal weights along averaging direction
    Kx = np.array([[-1, -1, -1],
                   [ 0,  0,  0],
                   [ 1,  1,  1]], dtype=np.float32)

    Ky = np.array([[-1,  0,  1],
                   [-1,  0,  1],
                   [-1,  0,  1]], dtype=np.float32)

    Gx = convolve2d(img, Kx, mode='same', boundary='symm')
    Gy = convolve2d(img, Ky, mode='same', boundary='symm')

    # Gradient magnitude (full and approximated)
    magnitude     = np.sqrt(Gx**2 + Gy**2)       # exact
    magnitude_L1  = np.abs(Gx) + np.abs(Gy)        # fast approximation

    # Threshold to get binary edge map
    magnitude_norm = magnitude / magnitude.max()
    edges = (magnitude_norm > threshold).astype(np.uint8) * 255

    return Gx, Gy, magnitude, edges

# Quick demo:
def demo_prewitt(img):
    Gx, Gy, mag, edges = prewitt_detector(img, threshold=0.15)
    show([img, np.abs(Gx), np.abs(Gy), mag/mag.max(), edges/255],
         ['Original', 'Prewitt Gx', 'Prewitt Gy', 'Magnitude', 'Edges'])

Section C — Sobel Detector

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# C. SOBEL EDGE DETECTOR
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def sobel_detector(img, threshold=0.1):
    """
    Sobel edge detector.
    The Sobel kernel = smoothing [1,2,1] × differentiation [-1,0,1].
    The central row/column gets double weight → more noise-robust than Prewitt.
    """
    # Sobel kernels
    Kx = np.array([[-1, -2, -1],
                   [ 0,  0,  0],
                   [ 1,  2,  1]], dtype=np.float32)

    Ky = np.array([[-1,  0,  1],
                   [-2,  0,  2],
                   [-1,  0,  1]], dtype=np.float32)

    Gx = convolve2d(img, Kx, mode='same', boundary='symm')
    Gy = convolve2d(img, Ky, mode='same', boundary='symm')

    magnitude = np.sqrt(Gx**2 + Gy**2)
    direction = np.arctan2(Gy, Gx)

    magnitude_norm = magnitude / magnitude.max()
    edges = (magnitude_norm > threshold).astype(np.uint8) * 255

    return Gx, Gy, magnitude, direction, edges


# Using OpenCV's built-in Sobel (faster for large images):
def sobel_opencv(img_uint8, threshold=50):
    """
    OpenCV implementation — expects uint8 input [0,255].
    ddepth=cv2.CV_64F to capture negative gradients (important!).
    """
    Gx = cv2.Sobel(img_uint8, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)  # dx=1, dy=0
    Gy = cv2.Sobel(img_uint8, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)  # dx=0, dy=1

    magnitude  = np.sqrt(Gx**2 + Gy**2)
    direction  = np.arctan2(Gy, Gx) * (180 / np.pi)  # radians → degrees

    edges = np.uint8(np.clip(magnitude, 0, 255))
    _, binary = cv2.threshold(edges, threshold, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)

    return Gx, Gy, magnitude, direction, binary

Section D — Marr-Hildreth (LoG) Detector

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# D. MARR-HILDRETH EDGE DETECTOR (Laplacian of Gaussian)
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def log_kernel(size=9, sigma=1.4):
    """
    Create a Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) kernel.
    Also known as the 'Mexican Hat' filter.
    
    LoG formula:
    ∇²g(x,y) = −(1/πσ⁴)[1−(x²+y²)/2σ²] exp(−(x²+y²)/2σ²)
    """
    ax = np.arange(-size // 2 + 1, size // 2 + 1)
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(ax, ax)
    r2 = xx**2 + yy**2
    sigma2 = sigma**2

    # LoG formula
    kernel = -(1 / (np.pi * sigma2**2)) * (1 - r2 / (2 * sigma2)) *              np.exp(-r2 / (2 * sigma2))

    # Zero-sum normalisation (important for stability)
    kernel -= kernel.mean()
    return kernel


def find_zero_crossings(log_response, threshold=0.01):
    """
    Find zero-crossings in the LoG-filtered image.
    A zero-crossing is where the sign changes between adjacent pixels.
    Only mark crossings where the slope |a + b| > threshold.
    """
    rows, cols = log_response.shape
    zero_crossings = np.zeros_like(log_response, dtype=np.uint8)

    for i in range(1, rows - 1):
        for j in range(1, cols - 1):
            patch = log_response[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2]
            min_val, max_val = patch.min(), patch.max()

            # Sign change exists in 3×3 neighbourhood
            if min_val < 0 and max_val > 0:
                slope = max_val - min_val   # measures ∝ |a+b|
                if slope > threshold:
                    zero_crossings[i, j] = 255

    return zero_crossings


def marr_hildreth(img, sigma=1.4, log_size=9, threshold=0.02):
    """
    Full Marr-Hildreth edge detector.
    Steps: Gaussian smooth → Laplacian → zero-crossings → threshold slope
    """
    # Method 1: Using scipy (efficient)
    log_response = gaussian_laplace(img, sigma=sigma)

    # Method 2: Explicit convolution with LoG kernel
    # kernel = log_kernel(log_size, sigma)
    # log_response = convolve2d(img, kernel, mode='same', boundary='symm')

    edges = find_zero_crossings(log_response, threshold=threshold)
    return log_response, edges


# Efficient separable 1D approach (as in lecture slides):
def marr_hildreth_separable(img, sigma=1.4):
    """
    Separable LoG:  ∇²g = gxx(x)·g(y) + g(x)·gyy(y)
    Uses 4 separable 1D convolutions — faster than 2D convolution.
    """
    from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter1d

    # ∂²/∂x² component: differentiate twice in x, smooth in y
    smooth_y   = gaussian_filter1d(img, sigma, axis=0)      # g(y) ∗ I
    d2x        = gaussian_filter1d(smooth_y, sigma, axis=1,
                                   order=2)                   # gxx(x) ∗ result

    # ∂²/∂y² component: smooth in x, differentiate twice in y
    smooth_x   = gaussian_filter1d(img, sigma, axis=1)      # g(x) ∗ I
    d2y        = gaussian_filter1d(smooth_x, sigma, axis=0,
                                   order=2)                   # gyy(y) ∗ result

    log_response = d2x + d2y    # ∇²g ∗ I = gxx∗g∗I + g∗gyy∗I
    edges = find_zero_crossings(log_response, threshold=0.005)
    return log_response, edges

Section E — Canny Edge Detector (from Scratch) 

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# E. CANNY EDGE DETECTOR — full implementation from scratch
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def non_maximum_suppression(magnitude, direction):
    """
    Thin edges to 1-pixel width by suppressing non-maximum pixels.
    For each pixel, we check its two neighbours along the gradient direction.
    If the pixel is NOT a local maximum, it is suppressed (set to 0).
    
    Gradient directions are quantised to 4 angles: 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°
    """
    H, W = magnitude.shape
    suppressed = np.zeros_like(magnitude)

    # Convert radians to degrees and wrap to [0, 180)
    angle = np.degrees(direction) % 180

    for i in range(1, H - 1):
        for j in range(1, W - 1):
            a = angle[i, j]

            # Determine neighbours along gradient direction
            if (0 <= a < 22.5) or (157.5 <= a < 180):
                # 0° — horizontal edge, check left/right
                q, r = magnitude[i, j+1], magnitude[i, j-1]
            elif 22.5 <= a < 67.5:
                # 45° — check top-right / bottom-left
                q, r = magnitude[i-1, j+1], magnitude[i+1, j-1]
            elif 67.5 <= a < 112.5:
                # 90° — vertical edge, check top/bottom
                q, r = magnitude[i-1, j], magnitude[i+1, j]
            else:
                # 135° — check top-left / bottom-right
                q, r = magnitude[i-1, j-1], magnitude[i+1, j+1]

            # Keep pixel only if it is a local maximum
            if magnitude[i, j] >= q and magnitude[i, j] >= r:
                suppressed[i, j] = magnitude[i, j]
            # else: suppressed[i, j] stays 0

    return suppressed


def hysteresis_thresholding(suppressed, low_threshold, high_threshold):
    """
    Two-threshold hysteresis:
    - Pixels > high_threshold  : STRONG edges (definitely edges)
    - Pixels < low_threshold   : Non-edges (discarded)
    - Between low and high     : WEAK edges (kept only if connected to strong)
    """
    H, W = suppressed.shape

    # Classify pixels
    STRONG = 255
    WEAK   = 50

    result = np.zeros_like(suppressed, dtype=np.uint8)
    result[suppressed >= high_threshold] = STRONG
    result[(suppressed >= low_threshold) & (suppressed < high_threshold)] = WEAK

    # Link weak edges connected to strong edges
    # Using iterative flood fill (BFS-like)
    from collections import deque

    final = np.zeros_like(result)
    final[result == STRONG] = STRONG

    queue = deque(zip(*np.where(result == STRONG)))  # start from all strong edges
    visited = (result == STRONG)

    while queue:
        i, j = queue.popleft()
        # Check all 8 neighbours
        for di in [-1, 0, 1]:
            for dj in [-1, 0, 1]:
                ni, nj = i + di, j + dj
                if 0 <= ni < H and 0 <= nj < W and not visited[ni, nj]:
                    if result[ni, nj] == WEAK:   # weak pixel connected to strong
                        final[ni, nj] = STRONG
                        visited[ni, nj] = True
                        queue.append((ni, nj))

    return final


def canny_from_scratch(img, sigma=1.0, low_t=0.05, high_t=0.15):
    """
    Full Canny edge detector implemented from scratch.
    
    Parameters:
        img    : float grayscale image [0,1]
        sigma  : Gaussian smoothing parameter (controls noise suppression)
        low_t  : low threshold for hysteresis [0,1]
        high_t : high threshold for hysteresis [0,1]
    Returns:
        edges  : binary edge map
    """
    # Step 1: Gaussian smoothing
    smoothed = gaussian_filter(img, sigma=sigma)

    # Step 2: Compute gradient using Sobel
    Kx = np.array([[-1,-2,-1],[0,0,0],[1,2,1]], dtype=np.float32)
    Ky = np.array([[-1,0,1],[-2,0,2],[-1,0,1]], dtype=np.float32)
    Gx = convolve2d(smoothed, Kx, mode='same')
    Gy = convolve2d(smoothed, Ky, mode='same')

    # Step 3: Magnitude and direction
    magnitude = np.sqrt(Gx**2 + Gy**2)
    direction = np.arctan2(Gy, Gx)

    # Normalise magnitude to [0,1]
    magnitude /= magnitude.max()

    # Step 4: Non-Maximum Suppression
    thin = non_maximum_suppression(magnitude, direction)

    # Step 5: Hysteresis Thresholding
    edges = hysteresis_thresholding(thin, low_t, high_t)

    return edges

Section F — Complete Demo (All Detectors)

Python# -----------------------------------------------------------
# F. FULL COMPARISON DEMO
# -----------------------------------------------------------

def compare_all_detectors(image_path):
    """Run all detectors on an image and display results side-by-side."""
    # Load image
    img_float = load_gray(image_path)
    img_uint8 = (img_float * 255).astype(np.uint8)

    # 1. Prewitt
    _, _, _, prewitt_edges = prewitt_detector(img_float, threshold=0.15)

    # 2. Sobel
    _, _, _, _, sobel_edges = sobel_detector(img_float, threshold=0.12)

    # 3. Marr-Hildreth (LoG)
    _, marr_edges = marr_hildreth(img_float, sigma=1.5, threshold=0.02)

    # 4. Canny from scratch
    canny_custom = canny_from_scratch(img_float, sigma=1.4,
                                       low_t=0.05, high_t=0.15)

    # 5. OpenCV Canny (for reference)
    #    cv2.Canny(img, threshold1, threshold2, apertureSize=3)
    canny_cv2 = cv2.Canny(img_uint8, 50, 150, apertureSize=3)

    # Display all results
    show(
        [img_float, prewitt_edges/255, sobel_edges/255,
         marr_edges/255, canny_custom/255, canny_cv2/255],
        ['Original', 'Prewitt', 'Sobel',
         'Marr-Hildreth', 'Canny (scratch)', 'Canny (OpenCV)'],
        figsize=(22, 4)
    )

# Quick test using a built-in image:
def quick_test():
    """Test with a synthetic image (no file needed)."""
    # Create a test image with shapes
    img = np.zeros((300, 300), dtype=np.float32)
    img[50:150, 50:150]  = 0.8   # white square
    img[120:250, 120:250] = 0.5   # grey square

    # Add Gaussian noise
    noise = np.random.normal(0, 0.05, img.shape).astype(np.float32)
    img_noisy = np.clip(img + noise, 0, 1)

    canny_result = canny_from_scratch(img_noisy, sigma=1.5, low_t=0.03, high_t=0.1)
    show([img_noisy, canny_result/255],
         ['Noisy Input', 'Canny Edges'], figsize=(10, 4))

quick_test()
